text: {"status":"ok","message-type":"work","message-version":"1.0.0","message":{"indexed":{"date-parts":[[2026,9,28]],"date-time":"2026-09-28T14:56:09Z","timestamp":1790607369605,"version":"4.1.0"},"reference-count":19,"publisher":"NGO "Research and Educational Innovation Center of Social Transformations"","issue":"27","license":[{"start":{"date-parts":[[2026,9,28]],"date-time":"2026-09-28T00:00:00Z","timestamp":1790553600000},"content-version":"unspecified","delay-in-days":0,"URL":"http:\/\/creativecommons.org\/licenses\/by\/4.0\/"}],"content-domain":{"domain":[],"crossmark-restriction":false},"short-container-title":["PMT"],"abstract":"<jats:p>Digital public services can reduce firms\u2019 administrative burdens, but their independent association with the productivity of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including microenterprises, remains insufficiently examined. The study aims to assess whether digital public service maturity is associated with SME labour productivity and whether this association persists after accounting for economic development. The analysis combines 2022 World Bank GovTech indicators and the United Nations Online Service Index with Eurostat SME productivity data for 2022\u20132023 and World Bank GDP per capita data for 2022 across 33 European countries. SME productivity is measured as value added per person employed; digital service maturity is represented by the Public Service Delivery Index (PSDI) and the Online Service Index (OSI) for 2022. The main hypothesis is that higher digital public service maturity is positively associated with SME productivity and remains significant after controlling for GDP per capita. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, ordinary least squares models, HC3 robust standard errors, diagnostics, and sensitivity analysis are applied. No statistically significant association between PSDI and SME productivity is identified. OSI is positive and significant in bivariate models, but its coefficient is no longer statistically significant after GDP per capita at purchasing power parity is included. Several service-specific GovTech indicators show pronounced ceiling effects and limited variation. The findings indicate that country-level digital service maturity scores should not be treated as stand-alone indicators of the productivity conditions faced by SMEs. Monitoring frameworks should complement maturity scores with measures of business uptake, interoperability, reliability, processing time, and administrative cost savings. The study\u2019s originality lies in jointly demonstrating the specification sensitivity of the OSI\u2013SME productivity association and the limited discriminatory capacity of service-specific GovTech indicators affected by ceiling effects. The conclusions are limited to the analysed indicators and sample and do not establish causal effects; future research should use repeated GovTech observations, purchasing-power-adjusted productivity measures, and firm-level service-use data.
